title: Health insurance before 65
teaches: How ACA marketplace premium credits work as a tax on income, the 400 percent cliff in 2026, what counts as income for them, and how to plan income in the years before Medicare

parts.title: A price that depends on your income

blocks.text: Anyone who stops working before 65 loses employer health insurance and isn't yet old enough for Medicare. For most, the answer is a plan bought on the marketplace set up by the Affordable Care Act, at HealthCare.gov or a state's own exchange, which in Washington is Washington Healthplanfinder.

The sticker prices are high, and they rise with age: a plan for a 60-year-old can cost nearly three times as much as the same plan for a 21-year-old.[^age-curve] A couple around 60 can easily face $20,000 to $30,000 a year for a mid-range plan. What they actually pay, though, depends on their income, through a premium tax credit that can cover most of the price. For someone living on savings, income is partly a choice, which makes this one of the largest numbers in an early-retirement plan that can be steered.

Everything in this lesson is for 2026. The rules changed at the start of the year, when a temporary expansion of the credits that ran from 2021 to 2025 ended, and Congress may change them again.[^enhanced] Check the current year's rules before planning.

parts.title: How the credit is worked out

blocks.text: Marketplace plans come in metal tiers, from bronze (cheapest, paying the smallest share of bills) through silver to gold. The marketplace picks a benchmark plan for you, the second-cheapest silver plan where you live, at your ages. It then sets how much of your income you are expected to pay towards it: in 2026, from 2.1 percent of income for a household just above the poverty line to 9.96 percent for one between three and four times it. The credit is the difference. Buy the benchmark and you pay the expected amount; buy a cheaper plan and you pay less, a dearer one, more.

The **poverty line** is an income set by the federal government each year by household size, and many programmes measure eligibility against it. The line used for 2026 coverage is $15,650 for one person and $21,150 for two. A couple with $60,000 of income is at 284 percent of it ($60,000 ÷ $21,150) and is expected to pay about 9.5 percent, $5,678; if their benchmark costs $24,000, the credit is $18,322.
Make a guess before moving the sliders: what does a couple at $84,000 of income pay for the benchmark, and what do they pay at $85,000?

blocks.caption: A couple's cost for the benchmark plan as their income rises, in 2026. Below: the federal income tax plus the extra premium on the next $1,000 of income. Shaded: below 138 percent of the poverty line, where Washington and other expansion states offer Medicaid instead.
blocks.task: Guess, then cross the 400 percent line and come back

blocks.text: Inside the credit range the premium works like a second income tax. Each extra dollar of income raises the expected payment, so the next $1,000 costs the federal tax on it plus up to about $180 of lost credit. Between about 200 and 300 percent of the poverty line, a couple in the 12 percent bracket pays 25 to 30 percent on the next dollar, counting both.

Above 400 percent of the poverty line, $84,600 for a couple in 2026, there is no credit at all. The couple with $84,000 of income and a $24,000 benchmark pays about $8,400, just under 10 percent of their income. At $85,000 they pay the full $24,000. That last $1,000 of income costs them more than $15,000.

The cliff hurts most for older couples, whose benchmark plans cost most, and in expensive areas. A couple of 63 in a costly county may face a benchmark of $30,000 or more, so a dollar over the line costs over $20,000. For a single person the line is $62,600. At that income a 40-year-old is expected to pay 9.96 percent, about $6,200, and their benchmark might cost only $6,000, so there is no credit to lose and no cliff at all.

At the bottom there is a second edge. In the 40 states and Washington, D.C., that expanded Medicaid, income below 138 percent of the poverty line ($29,187 for a couple) qualifies for Medicaid instead of a marketplace plan, and no credit is available. In the states that didn't, income below 100 percent usually gets neither.[^medicaid] Washington's Medicaid is called Apple Health; the course's Washington branch has a lesson on it and what it means for a retiree with savings.

The income the marketplace uses is modified adjusted gross income, MAGI: the adjusted gross income (AGI) on the tax return, with three things added back: the part of Social Security that isn't taxed, tax-exempt interest, and any foreign income excluded from tax. It counts wages, interest, dividends, capital gains, pension income, withdrawals from pre-tax accounts and Roth conversions.

It doesn't count money that isn't income: the basis of shares sold (what you paid for them, which comes back untaxed, lesson 7), cash in the bank, Roth contributions withdrawn, HSA money spent on health care, or a loan. So two couples who spend the same $80,000 can show very different MAGI. One sells $80,000 of shares with $60,000 of basis and draws on cash: MAGI $20,000, Medicaid range. Another takes $80,000 from an IRA: MAGI $80,000, near the cliff.

The credit is paid in advance, based on the income you predict when you enrol, and settled on the tax return the following spring.[^reconcile] Income that comes out higher than predicted means paying some or all of the credit back. A December Roth conversion that crosses the cliff by accident costs the whole year's credit.

This sets up a tension with lesson 10. Roth conversions in the early years fill the low brackets cheaply, but before 65 each converted dollar also raises the premium. At 25 to 30 percent combined, a conversion in the credit range can cost more than the 10 to 22 percent the money would probably pay if it were withdrawn later instead. Across the cliff it can cost far more.
A common plan for the years from stopping work to 65:

**Choose a MAGI target each year.** The cliff is the hard limit: crossing it by a dollar can cost thousands. Below it, each extra dollar converted costs 25 to 30 percent. If that money would otherwise pay 22 percent or more later, converting up to just under the cliff can still pay; if it would pay only 10 or 12 percent, a lower target that keeps more of the credit is better. Above 400 percent, if the household's income would be far over the line anyway, the cliff stops mattering and conversions are judged on tax alone.

**Fund spending from money that isn't income.** Cash, the basis in a taxable account, Roth contributions and conversions more than five years old (lesson 9) all buy groceries without raising MAGI. A conversion was counted as income in the year it was made, so spending it later doesn't count again. A taxable account with a high basis is especially useful here.

**Convert more from 65.** Once Medicare starts, the premium credit no longer matters, and the years from 65 to Social Security or to required withdrawals become the main conversion window, minding Medicare's surcharge on higher incomes, which lesson 12 explains. The surcharge looks back two years: income at 63 sets the premium at 65. Required withdrawals, the yearly withdrawals the law forces from pre-tax accounts from 73 or 75, close the window.

**Watch the year of stopping work.** A year with nine months of salary already has high income, so a credit based on it will be small. Many people keep the old employer's plan through COBRA[^cobra] for the rest of that year, and start marketplace coverage in January of the first full year without wages.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The ACA premium credit fills the gap between a benchmark plan's price and a set share of income, 2.1 to 9.96 percent in 2026.
In the credit range, each extra dollar of income costs tax plus lost credit, often 25 to 30 percent together.
Above 400 percent of the poverty line, $84,600 for a couple, the credit stops entirely.
Basis, cash, Roth contributions and HSA spending don't count as income, so spending and MAGI can differ widely.

blocks.caption: Six questions on health insurance before 65
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What is the benchmark plan used to work out the premium tax credit?
choices: The second-cheapest silver plan where you live, at your ages
The cheapest bronze plan in the state
items.why: The credit is the benchmark's price minus your expected contribution, whatever plan you then buy.

items.ask: A couple's income rises from $84,000 to $85,000 in 2026, crossing 400 percent of the poverty line. What happens to their credit?
items.why: In 2026 there is no credit above 400 percent of the poverty line, so the household pays the full price.

items.ask: Which of these raises MAGI for the marketplace?
choices: Spending cash from a savings account
items.why: A conversion is ordinary income. Roth contributions and cash are money already taxed and are not income.

items.ask: A couple sells $80,000 of shares with a $60,000 basis. How much does the sale add to MAGI?
items.why: Only the gain is income. The basis comes back without adding to MAGI.

items.ask: Inside the credit range, why can the next $1,000 of income cost 25 to 30 percent?
choices: Income tax plus a smaller credit as the expected contribution rises
items.why: The expected contribution rises with income, so the credit falls; that loss stacks on the income tax.

items.ask: Why is the year from 65 often a better time for large Roth conversions than the years before?
choices: The premium credit no longer depends on income
items.why: With Medicare, the marketplace credit is gone, so conversions are judged on income tax, and on the Medicare surcharge two years later.

summary: **Health premiums before 65 depend on income.** The credit is the benchmark price less a set share of income.
**In 2026 that share runs from 2.1 to 9.96 percent.** After the temporary expansion of 2021 to 2025 ended.
**The credit is a second income tax.** In the credit range the next dollar can cost 25 to 30 percent with federal tax.
**Above 400 percent of the poverty line, nothing.** $84,600 for a couple; a dollar over can cost $15,000 or more.
**MAGI isn't spending.** Basis, cash, Roth contributions and HSA spending pay bills without raising it.
**Plan a MAGI target each year to 65.** Convert less before Medicare and more after it.
**The credit is settled at tax time.** Income above the estimate means paying credit back.

enhanced.title: 2021 to 2025
enhanced.text: The American Rescue Plan of 2021 lowered the expected contributions, to nothing below 150 percent of the poverty line, and capped them at 8.5 percent of income with no upper limit, removing the cliff. The Inflation Reduction Act extended this through 2025. When it ended, the 2026 premiums of many households above 400 percent of the poverty line more than doubled. Whether it returns is a political question; check the year you plan for.

medicaid.title: Expansion
medicaid.text: The Affordable Care Act let states extend Medicaid to adults under 138 percent of the poverty line, with the federal government paying most of the cost. Washington did so in 2014. In the ten states that have not, adults under 100 percent of the poverty line usually qualify for neither Medicaid nor a marketplace credit.

reconcile.title: Settling up
reconcile.text: The marketplace pays the credit to the insurer each month based on your estimate; Form 8962 on the tax return compares it with what your actual income allowed. Under the budget act of July 2025, from 2026 there is no cap on how much of an over-paid credit must be repaid. Check the year's rules.

age-curve.title: The 3-to-1 age limit
age-curve.text: Federal rules cap the price for a 64-year-old at three times the price for a 21-year-old. On the federal curve, a 60-year-old pays 2.714 times the 21-year-old rate. Because the benchmark plan's price also rises with age, the credit grows alongside the sticker price, keeping the net cost tied to income for anyone under 400 percent of the poverty line.

cobra.title: COBRA
cobra.text: A federal law (the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1985) that lets someone leaving an employer with 20 or more workers keep the company health plan for up to 18 months, paying the full premium plus a 2 percent fee.
